sentences.text: Teratophoneus is a genus of tyrannosaurine theropod dinosaur whose name translates to "monstrous murderer" from Greek roots.
The single known species, T. curriei, honors the Canadian paleontologist Philip J. Currie.
The holotype, which is the specimen the species is based on, was not fully grown and measured roughly 6 meters in length with a mass of 667 kilograms.
Gregory S. Paul estimated that a fully grown adult could reach 8 meters long and weigh 2.5 metric tons.
Later analysis of the frontal bone size suggested the subadult was approximately 6.1 meters long and weighed 1 metric ton.
Researchers propose that the unusually deep skull might have supported stronger jaw muscles and a more powerful bite.
A bone bed containing four or five individuals aged between 4 and 22 years suggests these predators lived and died together.
Thomas D. Carr and colleagues formally established the genus and named it in 2011.
Fossils were unearthed in Utah, USA.
A new specimen was found in the Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument in 2017.
In 2021, fossils belonging to four or five individuals were described.
A 2021 study of a bone bed suggests Teratophoneus may have been a social pack-hunter.
Loewen et al. (2013) confirmed that Teratophoneus belongs to the tyrannosaurid subfamily Tyrannosaurinae.
Voris et al. (2020) placed Teratophoneus in a subclade with Dynamoterror and Lythronax, later named Teratophoneini in 2024.
Teratophoneus was closely related to the large tyrannosaurids Tarbosaurus and Tyrannosaurus, being more primitive than them but more advanced than Daspletosaurus.
Teratophoneus curriei lived approximately 77 to 76 million years ago during the middle of the Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous.
During its time, the site was located near the western coast of the Niobrara Sea, an inland sea that divided North America into Laramidia and Appalachia.
The dinosaurs lived on an ancient floodplain featuring peat swamps surrounded by highlands.
The Kaiparowits Formation paleofauna included chondrichthyan fish, frogs, salamanders, turtles, lizards, and crocodilians.
